newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Geneva breakthrough promises progress on landmines.
newsitem.headline: Geneva breakthrough promises progress on landmines.

text.p: The U.N.-sponsored Conference on Disarmament appointed a special co-ordinator on Thursday to try to launch global negotiations to ban landmines, which are blamed for killing 25,000 people a year.
In agreeing to the Western-backed move, non-aligned states cleared the way for the humanitarian question of landmines to be tackled separately from deadlocked nuclear issues, diplomats said.
The conference quickly named Australian ambassador John Campbell to the co-ordinator's post -- an encouraging choice for those campaigning for a quick, total ban.

The decision was made possible when Syria's delegate left the conference room, tacitly permitting a consensus the day before the 61-member body ends its second session of 1997. The final seven-week round starts on July 28.
The United States, Britain, France and Germany welcomed the breakthrough, but some non-aligned countries including India and Cuba expressed concern over the precedent set at the talks.

The arms talks in Geneva had been deadlocked since the start of the year by three groups of states -- each wanting its own favourite issue tackled first and blocking the others' pet topics to get its way.

The recognised nuclear powers -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France -- are keen to control nuclear materials like plutonium and highly-enriched uranium to keep new members out of the A-weapons club.

But India, a threshold nuclear power, and its Third World friends did not want to talk about non-proliferation or landmines unless the recognised nuclear states would agree to set themselves a timetable for total nuclear disarmament.

Caught between were middle-size states who struggled to find a way forward on land mines -- a heart-wrenching issue for Britain's Princess Diana and millions of ordinary people appalled by the carnage mines continue to cause long after wars are over.
Thursday's development raises their hopes that a total or partial ban on land mines may no longer be held hostage in the Geneva nuclear stand-off.
"We have a decision and we are pleased. But it is one small step," Katharine Crittenberger, acting head of the U.S. delegation, told Reuters.
"We broke a logjam and hope we can continue to take subsequent decisions. For the United States, of course, talks on fissile material are next," she added.
Crittenberger said Washington hoped the special co-ordinator could make a quick report which would lead to setting up a formal negotiating committee on landmines.
But the issue has a stalemate of its own.

Canada, which has no use for landmines, has been lining up like-minded signatories for an idealistic total ban, even though there is no hope that Russia and China, which have long land borders to defend, will take the pledge.
The United States, the key arbitrator, has decided that a total ban by only part of the world would be of little value and is insisting that Geneva is the only forum that counts.

With both China and Russia as members, the Geneva talks will have to come to grips with their concerns and seek a compromise, which could mean a partial or phased abolition of mines and restrictions or a ban on their export to Third World war zones.
China's ambassador Sha Zukang said Beijing favoured a phased landmines ban "but cannot agree to any immediate total ban".

Australia's Campbell, the new co-ordinator, was not in Geneva on Thursday -- he was at a landmines conference in Brussels where 86 countries have now signed a preliminary document for the Canadian-sponsored total ban scorned by Washington.
"I will pass the news on to him in Brussels," an Australian delegate told the U.N. talks. "I know he will be surprised."
